extracted.intended_audience: students and coaches preparing for mathematical olympiads / advanced high-school and undergraduate problem solvers
extracted.subtask_description: Techniques, theorems, and solution-patterns for solving and constructing rigorous solutions to geometry and trigonometry olympiad-style problems (power of a point, radical axis, dissections, regular polygons, constructions, telescoping trig sums).

rubrics_metrics.name: Radical center / concurrency of radical axes
rubrics_metrics.description: For three circles whose centers are not collinear, the radical axes of the three pairs are concurrent at the radical center. If the centers are collinear the radical axes are parallel or may coincide; if they coincide the circles are called coaxial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this property to deduce common intersection points of pairwise radical axes (useful in problems involving multiple circles). The page uses it to show concurrency of MN, PQ, and RS in intersecting-circle configurations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power of a point as a unifying tool
rubrics_metrics.description: The power of a point relative to a circle (products of directed segments from the point to intersection points or tangent length squared) is a versatile tool for proving tangency, concurrency, equalities, and metric relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply IA·IA' = R^2 − OI^2 for exterior/interior points, compare powers with respect to multiple circles to deduce radical axes, or combine with tangent-chord relations. Examples: derivation of Euler's relation and arguments about tangency and radical axes in the semicircle/DE example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving tangency via perpendicularity to radius/diameter
rubrics_metrics.description: A line is tangent to a circle at a point if and only if it is perpendicular to the radius (or diameter) at the point of contact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In practice prove DE is tangent by showing DE ⟂ OD (where O is the center) or that DE ⟂ diameter BE. Used in the semicircle example where midpoint-of-arc gives OD ⟂ AC and DE ∥ AC, hence DE ⟂ OD.

rubrics_metrics.name: Radical axis passes through midpoint of common external tangent
rubrics_metrics.description: If two circles have a common external tangent, the radical axis passes through the midpoint of the common tangent segment between tangency points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this when two circumcircles have a common tangent: locate radical axis by midpoint of the common tangent (example: BF passes through midpoint of DE).

rubrics_metrics.name: Euler relation in triangle: OI^2 = R(R − 2r)
rubrics_metrics.description: In a triangle with circumcenter O, incenter I, circumradius R and inradius r, the distance satisfies OI^2 = R(R − 2r).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derive using power of I with respect to circumcircle: IA·IA' = R^2 − OI^2; compute IA = r / sin(A/2) and IA' = 2R sin(A/2) (via angle bisector / law of sines) and substitute. The page shows the full step-by-step derivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cut polygons into triangles then reduce to rectangles/squares (Bolyai–Gerwin dissection method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any polygon can be cut into finitely many triangles (using diagonals). Triangles can be transformed into rectangles, and rectangles into squares; hence any two polygonal surfaces of equal area can be reassembled into each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use congruences, flips, and local rearrangements (e.g., triangle→rectangle construction, rectangle→square via chosen square intersecting midpoints) to perform finite dissections. The page outlines a constructive path and references the Bolyai–Gerwin theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inductive construction for dissecting an equilateral triangle into n equilateral triangles (n ≥ 6)
rubrics_metrics.description: Base decompositions into 6, 7, and 8 equilateral triangles exist; given a decomposition into n, one can obtain a decomposition into n+3 by subdividing one triangle into four.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the shown base cases and the local subdivision trick (cut one equilateral triangle into 4 smaller ones) to reach any n ≥ 6 by induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partition-and-count technique for extremal/combinatorial geometry
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide a configuration into a bounded number of regions/polygons and bound the quantity of interest locally in each region to obtain a global contradiction or bound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 9×9 chessboard problem — partition into 25 polygons, bound red squares per piece, derive contradiction if overall count too large. Useful for extremal coloring/packing problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graph/tree representation and limb/big-limb argument for polyomino tiling problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Represent touching-square-cell animals by a graph of cell-centers and edges between neighboring cells, cut cycles to form a tree, define limbs (components after deleting a vertex) and big limbs (limbs with ≥ threshold size) and use tree structure to bound sizes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to bound size of a primitive dinosaur: at most one big limb per vertex; find vertex with no big limbs by walking inward along big limbs; bound total vertices by counting limbs of bounded size.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit polygon symmetries to produce constructions (regular polygons)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use rotational/reflection symmetries of regular polygons to transform diagonals and subfigures into one another; folding/physical models can illustrate or produce constructions (e.g., pentagon from trefoil-folded ribbon).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When constructing or proving properties of regular polygons, identify symmetry-induced congruences of diagonals/triangles; folding arguments often convert global symmetry into local congruences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Express chord lengths via circumradius and use trigonometric identities
rubrics_metrics.description: Chord length = 2R sin(arc_angle/2) (or appropriate angle measure); translate geometric length relations into trigonometric identities and simplify using double-angle/product-to-sum formulas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: for a regular 14-gon, express the three chord lengths as 2R sin(π/7), 2R sin(2π/7), 2R sin(3π/7) and reduce the algebra to obtain sum-of-squares identity. Useful for many regular-polygon metric problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Telescoping principle in trigonometric sums and products
rubrics_metrics.description: Write a sum or product as a telescoping expression ∑(F(k) − F(k−1)) or ∏(G(k)/G(k−1)) so most terms cancel and only boundary terms remain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply product-to-sum, subtraction formulas, or known function identities (e.g., for sin, cos, tan−1) to turn a sum into telescoping form. Examples include sums of cos kx and telescoping of arctangent sequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use tangent (arctangent) subtraction formula for telescoping arctan sums
rubrics_metrics.description: tan−1 u − tan−1 v = tan−1((u − v)/(1 + uv)), so if (u − v)/(1 + uv) matches given summand, the sum telescopes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: set ak = tan−1 k so that tan(ak+1 − ak) = 1/(k^2 + k + 1); then ∑ tan−1(1/(k^2+k+1)) = tan−1(n+1). Useful for sums of inverse tangents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reflective method to construct or minimize broken-line paths
rubrics_metrics.description: To minimize AM + MB with M constrained to a line l, reflect B across l to C and take M as intersection of AC with l; then AM + MB = AC minimal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reflection to convert path-minimization to straight-line distance problems. Also constructive: reflect and intersect to build the minimizing point with ruler/compass.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixed-opening compass translation construction
rubrics_metrics.description: With a compass of fixed radius a, translate a point by a given vector by reducing to the case where segment lengths equal a using constructed auxiliary points at distance a and then composing equal-length translations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct points at distance a from vertices or endpoints and use sequences of equal-length vector translations to effect arbitrary vector translations under the fixed-radius constraint (described in the 1977 Bundeswettbewerb example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pompeiu-type and triangle-inequality technique for Fermat/Torricelli point
rubrics_metrics.description: The Fermat/Torricelli point of an acute triangle minimizes the sum of distances to the vertices and is characterized by 120° angles; proofs use equilateral-triangle constructions, Pompeiu's theorem (BQ+CQ ≥ QD), and triangle inequality to show minimality and uniqueness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Either use a physical equilibrium argument (weights suspended at vertices) or a geometric inequality argument (introduce equilateral triangle and apply Pompeiu + triangle inequality) to identify and justify the minimizer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correspondence between tetrahedron properties and associated parallelepiped
rubrics_metrics.description: A tetrahedron inscribed in a parallelepiped has properties reflected in the parallelepiped: orthogonal tetrahedron ⇔ rhomboidal parallelepiped (faces are rhombi); isosceles/equifacial tetrahedron ⇔ right parallelepiped (face diagonals equal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To prove orthogonality or equality-of-edges properties, inscribe tetrahedron in a carefully chosen parallelepiped and use planar/diagonal perpendicularity or equality arguments; use perpendiculars to faces to transfer statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affine invariance of volume ratios (use in tetrahedron/cube arguments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Volumes and ratios between sub-volumes determined by affinely related cuttings are preserved under affine maps; thus volume fractions computed in the unit cube (or regular figures) hold after any affine deformation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use simple models (unit cube with a regular tetrahedron) to compute volume ratios, then claim the same ratios for any affine image, simplifying volume computations in general cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use midpoints/perpendicular bisectors and congruences in constructive dissections
rubrics_metrics.description: Strategically choose lines intersecting sides at midpoints and use congruent triangles/quadrilaterals and flips to reassemble parts (e.g., rectangle→square construction via midpoint intersection XY with CD).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When performing dissections, aim to create pairs of congruent pieces (by midpoint/angle equalities) so simple cuts and flips yield the desired reassembly; the page gives concrete constructions and figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduce geometric metric identities to trigonometric sums and compute via product-to-sum
rubrics_metrics.description: Translate geometry length/angle identities into sums of sines/cosines and use standard trigonometric identities (double-angle, product-to-sum, symmetry of sine/cosine values) to simplify.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: sum of sin^2 terms for chords in a regular polygon reduced to a sum involving cosines, then manipulated using product-to-sum and cancellation; a standard pattern for many regular-polygon identities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem-catalogue style: present many exercises focused on a technique
rubrics_metrics.description: After introducing a technique (power of point, dissections, telescoping, etc.), present a curated list of problems that illustrate variations and strengthen mastery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the problem lists as checkpoints: if you can solve several of the listed exercises using the introduced techniques, you have internalized the method. The page supplies many such exercises grouped by topic.
